# CabinetOS

> **The record of what was decided, and why: look things up here, do not
> read it through.** It holds every decision from the project's start
> (2026-09-13) to 2026-10-23 with the research behind it, and is far too
> long to read whole. A contributor needs CONTRIBUTING.md,
> docs/ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/lessons/; their rules point to the section
> here that explains each one. A session searches it for the question in
> hand (the Index below lists them).
>
> **Starting a session?** `docs/NEXT-SESSION.md` is the short version: what
> state things are in, what to pick up, and the things that waste a day if
> nobody says them. This file is the record; that one is the handover.
> Rewrite it at the end of a session.
>
> **Cabinet, the Apple TV, iPhone and Mac app CabinetOS was ported from, is
> retired.** Until 2026-10-19 this note called it shipping and its source
> required reading. What Cabinet is now: docs/CABINET.md (Cabinet Go,
> unfinished). The map of the Apple apps' source: docs/history/CABINET.md.
> Where a line below says Cabinet or tvOS does something, it describes the
> apps as they were.
>
> This file is frozen since 2026-10-23: nothing new goes in it. New decisions
> are one small file each in docs/decisions/ (CLAUDE.md, rule 7;
> docs/decisions/README.md has the template and the index). When your work
> relies on a decision here, move it there and leave a one-line pointer in
> its place. A line that becomes untrue is rewritten or deleted, not
> annotated (CLAUDE.md, rule 5).
>
> **Since 2026-10-17 (#398, "Audit the code and restructure it for
> contributors (main.cpp is 20,000 lines)"):** this file is the record of what
> was decided and why; for what the code does today, the code and
> CONTRIBUTING.md are current. Stale lines below carry a dated note rather
> than an edit, which was this file's rule until 2026-10-23. Since
> 2026-10-11 (open question 12b,
> #344, "GameCube: a save restored from RomM never reaches Dolphin (card.raw vs
> card.USA.raw)"), Cabinet is a reference, not a constraint: read
> docs/history/CABINET.md for how a problem was solved before; Cabinet's own
> source is not required reading.

---

## Index

Added 2026-10-17 (#398, "Audit the code and restructure it for contributors
(main.cpp is 20,000 lines)"). GitHub does not render this file (it is
nearly 1 MB), so search it: a section by its heading (`## Hardware`), a
question by its number (`### 32.`). **Question numbers never change**: the
code cites them more than a hundred times.

### The sections, in order

- **Where the project is**: where the current state is kept now.
- **What CabinetOS is**: the product, the input model, the experience target.
- **Hardware**: the target, and the reference console (an A9 Max since
  2026-09-17).
- **The backend model**: RomM is the single source of truth for the library.
- **The frontend**: one visual language with the Cabinet apps, as first
  planned.
- **Reference implementations and upstreams**: what to read before
  inventing anything.
- **The update model**: one version number for the whole system.
- **Emulation**: native emulators, how Cabinet did it, core parity (overtaken
  since 2026-10-11).
- **How Cabinet hosts cores**: read from Cabinet's source; the shape of one
  C++ frontend with cores as data.
- **Controls: what CabinetOS inherits, and what it cannot**: players, the
  in-game shortcuts, and the dated screen decisions filed under it (the
  launch screen, Home and the top bar, the Dreamcast, PSP and N64 fixes,
  frame pacing, the emulator settings audit, the emulator queue, PS2's
  BIOS, time played).
- **Developer mode**: superseded; kept as history.
- **Staying current with Bazzite**: the base pinned by digest, moving the
  pin, and fixes waiting for a stable base (gamescope's crash when a game's
  window closes, 2026-10-22).
- **Measured behaviour**: the first booted image, the A9 Max measured,
  every platform run once, a start with no display answering.
- **Branding and the boot experience**: the palette.
- **The design system**: Cabinet's design, written out.
- **The frontend toolkit**: why C++20, SDL3 and a UI layer of its own.
- **Licensing, and the constraint it puts on the project**.
- **Non goals**.
- **Constraints and principles**: the numbered rules CONTRIBUTING.md cites.
- **Phase plan**: history; its status lines say so at its top.
- **Open questions**: the 56 below, plus two unnumbered sections ("Prior
  art: how Cabinet and Grout already do this", after question 13, and
  "PSP save sync, BUILT AND PROVEN 2026-09-17", after question 18).

### The open questions, and where each ended

Each status is the question's own words, read from the whole question: a
status line written when a question was raised is often overtaken further
down. "Look now at" is where the code or a later decision moved on.

- **1. How much of KDE Plasma can actually be removed?** "Unresolved", to be
  settled in Phase 2, which never came back to it. Plasma stays installed
  and unreachable; *Measured behaviour* found packages that never run cost
  nothing, and the toolkit chosen was not Qt. Look now at:
  `build_files/strip-desktop.sh`.
- **2. Does removing `steam` also remove the controller udev rules?**
  "RESOLVED by the first build": "no, controller support is intact". The
  `steam` package is kept again since 2026-10-03 for the Steam entry
  (question 37). Look now at: `build_files/strip-steam.sh`.
- **3. `bazzite` or `bazzite-deck` as the base?** "RESOLVED: stay on plain
  `bazzite` and write our own session". Still true; since 2026-10-03 the
  image also carries bazzite-deck's gamescope session, for the Steam entry
  only. Look now at: `build_files/install-steam-session.sh`, question 37.
- **4. Bundle libretro cores directly, or build on RetroDECK?** "RESOLVED in
  Phase 0: bundle directly, as `.so` files". True for the 22 libretro cores;
  Switch, PS3, Xbox, Xbox 360 and Wii U run as separate programs. Look now
  at: questions 21 and 32.
- **5. Anaconda ISO vs. a plain disk image for installing to real
  hardware.** "ANSWERED 2026-10-07: keep the ISO, automated down to one
  question", and built the same day. What the ISO builder will not change is
  #284 ("Installer: what the ISO builder will not let us change"), closed as
  cosmetic. Look now at: `disk_config/iso.toml`.
- **6. `/opt` mutability.** "Left at Bazzite's default". Nothing needed it:
  the emulators built into the image live under `/usr/lib/cabinetos/`.
- **7. OS branding in `/usr/lib/os-release`.** Its status line, "Deferred to
  Phase 8", is stale: built by #137 ("Name CabinetOS in the system's version
  info"), the cosmetic fields only, `ID` stays `bazzite`. Look now at:
  `build_files/brand-os-release.sh`.
- **8. How do we get a shell before Phase 6 ships developer mode?**
  "RESOLVED: SSH is on from the start"; the debt was "PAID 2026-10-07
  (#134)" ("A shipping image without the development shell"): Developer
  access, off by default. The row is in About (seven presses on Version),
  not "Settings, System" as the question says. Look now at:
  docs/SETTINGS.md, "Developer access".
- **9. How a person reaches their own files, and how it authenticates.**
  "ANSWERED 2026-09-19": a visible row, a generated password, SFTP and not a
  shell. Built as File access, under Storage. Binding it to the home network
  only was never decided. Look now at: docs/SETTINGS.md, "File access".
- **10. Waking the machine, and turning the TV on.** "Superseded 2026-09-24
  (#81): HDMI-CEC is shelved and its row is gone." (#81: "Docs: out-of-date
  lines in PROJECT.md and NEXT-SESSION.md".) Its blanking half was built
  without CEC, under 10b. Look now at: question 31, "HDMI-CEC IS SHELVED".
- **10b. The console never sleeps, and never blanks the screen.** Pixel
  shift, dim and blank "BUILT 2026-09-22"; the Power menu and the save
  before shutdown were built 2026-09-22/23, further down. Still open: the
  sleep each machine can really do. Look now at: #132 ("Offer the sleep this
  machine can really do"); docs/SETTINGS.md, "Turn off screen after".
- **11. NVIDIA hardware.** "Out of scope until there is hardware that needs
  it"; closed by decision 2026-10-12 in #300 ("An NVIDIA computer: what
  CabinetOS does on one today, and whether to offer an NVIDIA image"):
  CabinetOS is for AMD Radeon, and a fork is welcome.
- **12. In-process cores for the heavy systems, or separate processes?**
  "RESOLVED ... in-process, all of them" now holds only for PS2 (PCSX2 as a
  library) and GameCube and Wii (the Dolphin core). Switch, PS3, Xbox, Xbox
  360 and Wii U run as separate programs. Look now at: question 32.
- **12b. Every platform audited, and the order the rest get built.** The
  audit and the order were decided 2026-09-20; every heavy system on it has
  since been built; Jaguar, ColecoVision and Game & Watch will not be. Look
  now at: questions 32 to 36; question 22 for the Library filter it waited
  for, built there (#117, "Library shows only the systems this console can
  play").
- **13. Building the same cores for Linux x86-64.** "Repo layout DECIDED.
  SCOPED IN PHASE 0". Built since: every libretro core pinned and built in
  CI, file saves synced (2026-09-19), states sent to RomM (2026-09-23). Its
  "Still open" list is mostly Cabinet's side, no longer a constraint since
  2026-10-11. Look now at: CONTRIBUTING.md, "The rules";
  `frontend/src/savetable.cpp`.
- **Prior art: how Cabinet and Grout already do this** (not a question). A
  record, "Read 2026-09-13". Its "offline is one signal" is overtaken by
  question 29, and Download All was never built.
- **14. User-selectable game storage.** Its status line, "Mostly DECIDED",
  is stale: built 2026-09-19, revised 2026-09-25 (kept games fill the main
  drive first) and 2026-10-04 (#236, "Drives: use Linux's own format (ext4)
  for extra drives, shared with Steam"). Moving games between drives was
  never built. Look now at: docs/SETTINGS.md, "Storage".
- **15. A phone companion page for first run.** "NOT ADOPTED YET": deferred,
  never built and never closed. First run now pairs with RomM by QR code on
  the console's own screen. Look now at: question 15b.
- **15b. First run, and the one input that can be guaranteed.** Its status
  line says "Not built"; further down, "THE FOUR MECHANISMS ARE BUILT" and
  "AND THE SCREENS ARE BUILT TOO", both 2026-09-20. Its "What is still owed"
  list is stale. Look now at: `frontend/src/setup.cpp`.
- **16. Is a mouse supported, or not?** "ANSWERED 2026-09-19: option 2": a
  mouse "moves focus and clicks the focused thing, and nothing else". The
  code does that in first run only; elsewhere a click wakes the screen. The
  pointer itself is hidden since 2026-10-18 (#509, a PS5 pad's touchpad drew
  gamescope's arrow). Look now at: the input-model table in "What CabinetOS
  is", never amended (it carries a dated note).
- **17. Wi-Fi credentials on a controller-only console.** "The mechanism is
  DECIDED"; the polkit rule "SHIPPED 2026-09-20", and Wi-Fi is built in
  first run and in Settings. The password: "REVERSED 2026-09-24", masked,
  with the last character shown. Hidden networks are not built. Look now at:
  docs/SETTINGS.md, "Network".
- **18. The on-disk layout.** "DECIDED" 2026-09-17, "BUILT 2026-09-18".
  "REVERSED 2026-09-19: releasing the last keep DELETES." Its "What is still
  not built" list is built now. Look now at: `frontend/src/storage.h`,
  `locations.h`.
- **PSP save sync, BUILT AND PROVEN 2026-09-17** (not a question). The first
  directory save: sent to RomM and back byte-identical. "Still open": under
  a headless capture the core sometimes never starts. Look now at:
  `frontend/src/saves.cpp`, `savetable.cpp`.
- **19. Systems this console has and Cabinet does not.** "Raised and DECIDED
  by MMagTech, 2026-09-17": CabinetOS may carry systems Cabinet does not.
  PS3 built 2026-09-28 (#171, "New systems 2: PlayStation 3 (RPCS3)"). Its
  rule that core parity "still binds absolutely" was overtaken on 2026-10-11
  (question 12b). Updates and DLC wait: #181 ("Updates and DLC as separate
  files in RomM (Switch, PS3, Xbox 360)").
- **20. Vulkan, and how the host should choose a graphics API.** "BUILT

- **21. Emulators that are not cores, and why they cannot be baked into the
  image.** "DECIDED and BUILT the same day" (2026-09-18): a pinned Flatpak
  list installed at first boot; "RPCS3 leaves Flathub, 2026-09-28" for the
  image. What the screen says while they download is "NOT SETTLED". Look now
  at: `system_files/usr/share/cabinetos/flatpaks.list` (xemu and Eden).
- **23. One quality setting for the whole console, instead of emulator
  menus.** Its status line says "Not designed, not built"; it was designed

  quality phase 3: lower a struggling game's level by itself (the drop

- **22. What the console does when the server is away** (it comes after 23

- **24. Will gamescope composite our overlay over a window we do not own?**

  "TWO PATHS ARE ACCEPTED". Built for the separate programs 2026-09-28 and
  for PS2 2026-10-04 (#226, "PS2: show the picture without copying every

- **25. Save states, and whether the modern systems should have them at

- **26. Account switching, and what a console's version of it is.** "DECIDED

- **27. A one-line change ships half a gigabyte, because the image is one

- **29. Offline is not one fact, and the console has three networks to be

- **30. The console re-does work it already did, every boot.** Opens "NOT

- **49. PS Vita (Vita3K), issue #198** ("Research: PS Vita through Vita3K,
  and whether touch rules it out"). Researched 2026-10-19, not decided: the
  first four tests pass on paper; recommended no for now, because Sony's
  PS TV list assumes a touch pointer Vita3K lacks (Vita3K/Vita3K#3707), and
  no gyro. The A9 hand test waits for a time he names. Addendum the same
  night, his "how vital is that pointer?": a pointer is needed in play for
  at least one in ten of Sony's passed games; no frontend gives Vita3K a stick
  pointer (everyone has a touch surface); downloads are mostly Android; the
  console could build one as a virtual touch screen (medium). Still no for
  now, upstream first; his call: ask Vita3K or build it here. **Decided
  2026-10-20: a go**, the console's own pointer, by "Decided, 2026-10-20: the
  build plan" at the end of the question. **Built 2026-10-21** (#540, "PS
  Vita through Vita3K, played as a PlayStation TV"), unattended:
  "Built, 2026-10-21" after the plan says what the build found and what was
  checked. The probe passed on the TV; the hand test waits for him.
- **50. Nintendo 3DS (Azahar's libretro core).** Asked 2026-10-19, no issue.
  Researched the same night, not decided: Azahar's own core, pinnable at its
  2126.2 tag, fits the core host on Vulkan as it is; the touch screen is the
  DS's right-stick rule by the core's default; no states, by question 25;
  only decrypted cartridge dumps play. Recommended go with conditions: the
  build with its key blob off, no network for games (Azahar has no switch),
  an A9 test of Vulkan's frame pacing (azahar-emu/azahar#2093), and his
  legal call. With it, a touchpad as a second way to touch (the core takes
  it beside the stick, unlike melonDS, #288); gyro as a later piece of its
  own. His server has no 3DS games. **Go given the night of 2026-10-19,
  with the conditions; built (the core's arm, the catalog row, the levels,
  saves the PSP way, the encrypted-dump and CIA refusal, games given no
  network by a patch), #524 ("Nintendo 3DS through Azahar's own libretro
  core (decrypted dumps)"). On 2026-10-20: states yes, by his decision (the
  exception to question 25), side by side, levels 1x, 3x and 6x; tested on
  the TV with three of his games on Vulkan; CIAs hidden; conditions 4 and 5
  met by his go for the testing image ("Build the damn thing already").
  On the TV in 2026.10.20.5: every 3DS game after the first used the first
  game's folders, fixed by a second patch (#534, "Azahar patch: each game
  sets its own folders (until Azahar fixes SetUserPath)"); a toggled L3
  swap decided, then dropped (a third patch), so L3 stays held.**
- **51. Vectrex screen overlays, issue #224** ("Vectrex: the cartridges'
  screen overlays"). Researched 2026-10-19, not decided: Cabinet's 38 sheets
  are libretro/overlay-borders' `Game Overlay` folder, byte for byte (MIT,
  vector recreations by THK and Gigapig of HyperSpin); the designs are GCE's
  and Smith Engineering's now, not public domain, allowed non-commercially by
  Jay Smith's second-hand, undated permission, the one docs/LICENCES.md
  already uses for the system ROM; ten sheets carry other companies' marks.
  Recommended: ship that set at `385490fa8`, fetched at build time, 25 retail
  sheets and 3 variants drawn, the invented ones off, alpha-composited at
  opacity 1 over the core's picture. RetroArch and Bazzite ship none;
  Batocera ships the same sheet art inside Duimon's CC BY-NC-ND console
  bezels, in four optional sets. Decided late that day: an Overlays
  On / Off row in the Vectrex pause menu, kept per system like a look,
  default On, reversing the morning's "no row". The legal footing:
  decided go the same night; #224 is buildable as written.
- **52. Genie Mode: cheats, opt-in per person.** MMagTech's brief of
  2026-10-20, discussed 2026-10-20 and 2026-10-21, no issue. **Paused by
  him, not decided whether to build; not to be raised until he raises it.**
  If it goes ahead: per person; cheats chosen before launch only, never
  mid-game, and remembered per person and game; what a cheat changed can
  stay in saves and states; no achievements in a play with a cheat on.
  Open: where on the game page cheats are chosen (no new row, no more icons
  by the title), the Settings row, the cup's look while off, marking states
  made with cheats, and the phase order (he leans toward codes through the
  core first).
- **53. Gameplay recording, and clips in RomM.** MMagTech's proposal of
  2026-10-21, reviewed the same day, no issue. **Paused by him until RomM
  answers:** RomM has nowhere to keep a person's clips, and the console
  manages nothing RomM should (his rule). He commented on rommapp/romm#5135
  with an implementation sketch the same day, and would build RomM's side
  himself as a pull request if RomM wants one. The console side is
  feasible: gamescope's PipeWire stream for every game, encoded on the
  Radeon, paused whenever the game is not on screen. Open: RomM's answer,
  clip length and bitrate (RomM's upload limit decides them), sound, the
  menu rows, Remote Play, and the shortcut over emulators run as programs.

## What CabinetOS is

CabinetOS is a console operating system for generic x86-64 hardware.

The user experience target is a PlayStation or an Xbox, not a Linux PC. You
press the power button, the frontend appears, and everything from that point on
is driven with a controller.

The user never sees:

- a desktop
- a terminal or console
- a package manager
- a file browser
- a Linux error message

### The trigger channel, and why answering it wrongly is worse than silence

**Found 2026-09-19 by MMagTech, who said the shoulder buttons did not work.**

libretro has a third analogue index, `RETRO_DEVICE_INDEX_ANALOG_BUTTON`, and it
is not a stick: its `id` is a joypad button id, so L2 is 12 and R2 is 13. A
callback that tests for the LEFT index and treats everything else as the right
stick answers *"how far is the left trigger pressed"* with **where the right
stick is sitting**. Two faults in one line — the triggers cannot be pressed,
and the right stick drives them.

**And it is worse than returning nothing.** Flycast reads the analogue value
first and falls back to the digital L2/R2 bit **only when that value is exactly
zero**. Cabinet answers this index with a plain `0` and therefore works, by
taking the fallback. A real pad's right stick rests a few hundred counts off
centre; that is not zero, so it reads as *"the trigger is very slightly
pressed"* and suppresses the fallback entirely. **A bug that needed stick drift
to appear.**

CabinetOS now carries a real analogue value rather than Cabinet's zero —
`PadState` has `leftTrigger` and `rightTrigger` — so a pad with sprung triggers
gives a Dreamcast a continuous throttle, and one with switches, which is what a
Switch Pro Controller's ZL and ZR are, gives it 0 or full.

#### A button that does nothing is usually correct

A RetroPad has sixteen inputs and a real machine has fewer, so a press that
does nothing is normally right and looks exactly like a fault. **The Dreamcast
controller has no shoulder BUTTONS at all** — its L and R are the analogue
triggers — so on a Switch Pro Controller the top shoulders are meant to be
silent and ZL/ZR are the triggers.

The console stopped leaving that to guesswork on 2026-09-19:
`RETRO_ENVIRONMENT_SET_INPUT_DESCRIPTORS` was accepted and thrown away, and is
now printed once per game, including the half nobody prints:

```
[input] port 0: ... B=A, A=B, X=Y, Y=X, L2 (trigger)=L Trigger, R2 (trigger)=R Trigger, Start=Start
[input] port 0 does nothing in this game: Select, L (shoulder), R (shoulder), L3 (stick click), R3 (stick click)
```

It earned its keep immediately: Metal Slug X binds **L3 to Select**, so the
L3+R3 overlay chord sends one stray press on its way to opening — which follows
the rule already chosen, and is now visible rather than theoretical.

### The input model

**The controller is the primary input device, and the only one the design may
assume exists.**

Every screen, every flow, and every recoverable error state must be fully
navigable with a controller alone. Any state the machine can reach where a
controller is not sufficient to continue is a bug, not a limitation. This is the
single constraint that most shapes the frontend: it rules out designs that are
only tolerable with a pointer, and it is why text entry gets an on-screen
keyboard rather than a text field and a shrug.

**A keyboard and mouse are supported, but never required.** If one is plugged
in, it should work — typing a RomM server address, a Wi-Fi password or a search
query is genuinely faster on a keyboard, and there is no reason to refuse it.

The distinction that matters:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Required** | Controller. Everything must work with one. |
| **Supported** | Keyboard and mouse. A convenience, never a dependency. |
| **Never** | A flow that *only* works with a keyboard or mouse. |

Since 2026-09-19 (open question 16): a mouse moves focus and clicks the focused
thing, and nothing else. The code does that in first run only
(setup.cpp:1637-1677); on every other screen a click only wakes the screen
(input.cpp:59-67). A keyboard works on every screen (input.cpp:144).

Concretely: the on-screen keyboard is the baseline for all text entry and is
always reachable. A physical keyboard types into the same field when present.
Neither implementation may be the only one.

## Hardware

**The target is x86-64 PC hardware, not one specific machine.**

**The reference machine changed on 2026-09-17, which is exactly what this
section said would happen.** It is now a **GEEKOM A9 Max — AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370
(Zen 5, 12 cores) with Radeon 890M integrated graphics (RDNA 3.5, 16 CUs).**

> **It is the A9 MAX, not the A9 Pro.** Written down as "A9 Pro" in twenty
> places from 2026-09-17 until 2026-09-20, when the machine was asked rather
> than remembered: `/sys/class/dmi/id/product_name` says `A9 Max`, which is the
> manufacturer's own string for the board. Corrected everywhere, and noted here
> so nobody helpfully corrects it back. A GEEKOM A9 Pro is a different machine. It replaces the Beelink
SER5 (Ryzen 5, Vega), which was only ever the spare box that happened to be
available.

> *"If the project works out, the hardware may change, and CabinetOS must not
> have quietly grown dependencies on this particular box in the meantime."* —
> written here in Phase 1, and now cashed in. Nothing had to change to move
> machines, which is the point of having said it.

**What moves with it:**

- **The performance floor moves a long way up.** Phase 8 exists to tune PS2,
  GameCube, Dreamcast and Naomi "on Vega integrated graphics". That premise is
  gone. The floor is now Zen 5 with a Radeon 890M, and Phase 8's targets should be
  re-read rather than inherited.
- **Everything keyed to "the SER5" now means this machine** — most importantly
  the decision that no UI is designed or tuned until CabinetOS is installed on
  it. That gate did not move, but the thing it waits for did.
- **PS3 becomes a hardware question that is ANSWERED.** MMagTech, 2026-09-17:
  *"ive seen numerous videos on youtube of it running ps3 including god of war
  3."* RPCS3 is CPU-bound rather than GPU-bound — the work is emulating the
  Cell's SPUs — and Zen 5 carries AVX-512, which is the instruction set that
  matters most for it. **Treat PS3 performance as settled and stop revisiting
  it.** What remains for PS3 is architectural and storage-shaped, not
  performance-shaped; see open question 12.

**What does NOT move:**

- **Still AMD**, so the base image stays plain `bazzite` and open question 11
  (NVIDIA) stays out of scope. No second image to build, sign and boot.
- **Still no wired CEC pin.** Essentially no x86 mini PC has one, so the USB
  adapter stays in the bill of materials.
- **Storage is unaffected.** A faster CPU does not make PS3's 307 GB, or its
  37 GB single title, any smaller.

**One thing to verify rather than assume when it arrives:** Strix Point is recent
enough that its graphics support depends on a current Mesa and kernel. Bazzite
44 is Fedora 44 with Mesa 26.2, which should be comfortable — but "should be" is
the phrase this project has learned to distrust, so boot it before believing it.

The original text follows, because the reasoning is still the rule:

The development and reference machine was a Beelink SER5 mini PC (AMD Ryzen 5,
Radeon Vega integrated graphics) because that is the spare box available. It is
not the product's definition. If the project works out, the hardware may change,
and CabinetOS must not have quietly grown dependencies on this particular box in
the meantime.

What follows from that:

- **The reference machine sets the performance floor, not the ceiling.** Phase 8
  tunes PS2, GameCube, Dreamcast and Naomi to run acceptably on Vega integrated
  graphics. Anything faster is a bonus, and nothing may *require* a specific GPU.
- **No machine-specific quirks in the image.** No SER5 firmware workarounds, no
  hard-coded device paths, no assumptions about a particular audio or network
  chip. If the SER5 needs something unusual, that is a strong signal the fix
  belongs upstream in Bazzite, not here.
- **Hardware capability is discovered, not assumed** — with one exception, HDMI-CEC,
  which is a requirement rather than a capability. See below.
- **AMD for now.** Bazzite publishes NVIDIA variants of its images, so an NVIDIA
  machine is a base-image change rather than a rewrite — but it doubles the
  images to build and test, so it stays out of scope until there is hardware
  that needs it. See open question 11.

### HDMI-CEC is a hard requirement

Since 2026-09-24 (open question 31, "HDMI-CEC IS SHELVED"): shelved, and its
Settings row is gone; build_files/require-cec.sh still keeps the CEC packages
in the image.

**The console must be able to turn the television on, and be woken by it.** That
is not a nicety. It is a large part of what separates a console from a computer
sitting under the telly, and this product is defined by that difference.

Treat it like the controller: a thing the design may assume exists.

#### A USB adapter is required, on essentially any mini PC

**The Beelink SER5 has no wired CEC pin. Neither does the GMKtec K11.** Nor do
almost any x86 mini PCs — the HDMI connector carries the CEC line, but the board
does not wire it to anything. This is close to universal and should be planned
for rather than checked hopefully.

So the hardware requirement is a **USB CEC adapter**, and it is part of the
bill of materials for any CabinetOS machine.

| Adapter | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Pulse-Eight** | The known good choice. Has a dedicated `inputattach` unit in the image. |
| RainShadow | Also has a unit present; untested here. |
| Ugreen | **Behaves inconsistently in native mode.** Avoid, or use legacy mode. |

#### Two modes, and they behave differently

Bazzite ships both CEC stacks, switched with `ujust cec-mode` or the Bazzite
Portal:

- **Legacy** — `libcec` and `cec-ctl`, driving the `cec-onboot`, `cec-onsleep`
  and `cec-onpoweroff` services. This is the mode for external USB adapters,
  and therefore **the mode that matters on x86**.
- **Native** — Valve's `linux-cec`/`cecd`, for devices with CEC wired into the
  kernel. **`cecd` is known to interfere with wakeup on HTPC setups using
  dongles**, which is exactly our configuration, so native is not the default
  to reach for here.

Native mode is also **incomplete in this image**: Bazzite's native mode enables
`steamos-manager-configure-cecd.service` alongside `cecd`, and `steamos-manager`
is `bazzite-deck`-only. Pulling it in would drag the SteamOS management layer
into the image, which constraint 4 rules out. Legacy adapter mode is the
supported path; this is recorded rather than fixed.

#### The packages are protected, by an assertion rather than a comment

Every package CEC needs looks like cruft in a package list — `v4l-utils` reads
as a webcam package, `linuxconsoletools` as a joystick utility — and both are
load-bearing. `build_files/require-cec.sh` names each one with its reason and
**fails the build** if any goes missing, whether by our hand or an upstream
change. Audited and confirmed present on the running image: `libcec`,
`v4l-utils`, `linux-cec`, `linuxconsoletools`, the four udev rules, and all
seven CEC systemd units.

#### CEC will not be tested by the author

**MMagTech is not buying a CEC adapter. Testing will come from other people.**
That is a fine arrangement and it has consequences worth stating plainly,
because they shape how the feature must be built:

- **The no-adapter path is the one that gets exercised daily**, on every machine
  the author owns. That is lucky — it is also the common case for anyone who
  has not bought an adapter yet — but it means the with-adapter path only ever
  runs on someone else's television.
- **CEC must never be able to break boot or the session.** A missing, unplugged
  or misbehaving adapter has to be a quiet no-op. If CEC code can hang startup
  when no adapter is present, the author will not see it; if it can hang startup
  when one *is* present, the author will not see that either.
- **The settings UI has to be self-explanatory**, because the person switching
  modes will be debugging their own television without the author watching. A
  mode switch that needs explaining is a mode switch that will be reported as
  broken.
- **There must be a way to get a useful report back.** Which adapter, which
  mode, which television, what happened. Developer mode's SSH is the obvious
  channel for anyone technical; for everyone else the UI should show enough
  state — adapter detected, mode, last CEC event — that a photograph of the
  screen is a useful bug report.
- **Be honest in the status.** A hard requirement nobody on the project can test
  is a hard requirement in name only until someone confirms it. Until then it is
  specified and implemented, not verified, and the phase notes should say so
  rather than implying otherwise.

#### CabinetOS must surface the mode switch itself

**CabinetOS removes the terminal, and with it `ujust` and the Bazzite Portal** —
both mechanisms Bazzite provides for choosing a CEC mode. Verified: `ujust` is
gone from the built image.

So mode selection has to exist in CabinetOS's own settings, or the choice is
unreachable on a finished machine. **Phase 7 task**, recorded there.

The reference implementation is `/usr/share/ublue-os/just/81-bazzite-fixes.just`,
which survives in the image even though `ujust` does not. It writes `CEC_MODE`
to `/etc/default/cec-control`, toggles the three legacy units against
`cecd.service`, handles the two `inputattach` templates, and writes a `cecd`
config with `logical_address = "playback"`, `suspend_tv = true` and
`allow_standby = false`.

## The backend model

**RomM is the single source of truth for the library.** CabinetOS is a client.

Everything comes from the RomM server over its REST API:

- games and ROM files
- artwork and metadata
- platform information
- firmware and BIOS files
- save files and save states

Authentication uses a **client API token** obtained through RomM's device
pairing flow, so that a machine with no keyboard can be authorised without
typing a password.

CabinetOS stores nothing the server does not already know, with two exceptions:

1. the local cache of downloaded games
2. emulator configuration

Games are downloaded on demand and cached locally, and can additionally be
**kept** — pinned to the internal drive so they are never re-fetched or evicted.
The user can see what is cached, what is kept, and how much space is free, and
can move games between the two. See *Emulation* for why the distinction matters.

Saves and save states sync back to the server, so a game started on Apple TV
can be continued on CabinetOS and vice versa. This bidirectional continuity is
the single most valuable feature of the product and should be treated as such
when trading off scope.

**2026-10-19:** the Apple TV app is retired. The continuity now runs between
CabinetOS consoles, and with Cabinet Go when it comes, which will read the same
save rows (docs/CABINET.md).

---

## The frontend

The frontend matches the existing Cabinet apps in visual language, navigation
feel and motion, so that the Apple TV app and CabinetOS read as one product
rather than two things that share a name.

**2026-10-19:** the Apple TV app is retired, and since 2026-10-11 Cabinet is a
reference, not a constraint. The look stays as it was taken; nothing has to
keep matching an Apple app.

Screens:

- **Home** — resume-first. What you were playing, continue it.
- **Browse** — by platform and by collection.
- **Game detail** — artwork and metadata.
- **In-game overlay** — reachable from a controller button without leaving the
  game. Offers save states, resume, and exit.
- **Settings** — account, storage, controllers, display, system update, and
  **About**, which carries the version and the credits (see *Branding*).
- **First run setup** — pairs with a RomM server. On-screen keyboard is the
  baseline; a physical keyboard types into the same field if one is attached.

The frontend is **owned, not skinned**. CabinetOS does not ship someone else's
frontend with a theme applied, because that makes the product's identity
hostage to an upstream project's design decisions.
